finding.claim: The /mirror endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL. The only validation is host.endswith('example.com'), which has no leading dot. An attacker can register a domain such as attackerexample.com, or use a host like evilexample.com that resolves to an internal IP, and the server will request it. The unused ALLOWED_SUFFIX constant (.example.com) shows the intended check was never applied. There is no scheme check, no port check, and no resolved-IP check, so DNS pointing at 169.254.169.254 or other internal addresses is also reachable. The check also accepts userinfo or subdomain tricks that still end in example.com.

trace.note: weak suffix check: endswith('example.com') without a dot boundary
request issued to the original attacker-supplied url

finding.guards_checked: Hostname suffix check at line 13 is bypassable (evilexample.com). ALLOWED_SUFFIX is defined but unused. There is no scheme allowlist, no IP/DNS-rebinding protection, and no port restriction. httpx does not follow redirects by default, so redirect-based bypass was not counted. /ping uses a hardcoded URL and is not vulnerable.

verdict.guard_found: Only host.endswith("example.com") at mirror.py:13 (no dot boundary); ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused; no scheme, port, or resolved-IP checks, and no auth or middleware in the file.
verdict.reason: The `url` query parameter (mirror.py:11) is attacker-controlled and reaches `c.get(url)` at mirror.py:16 guarded only by the bypassable suffix check at mirror.py:13, so an attacker can use a host like attackerexample.com or a domain that resolves to an internal IP.
